cards.back: Departing from what is normal or expected. Example: 'The aberrant weather patterns observed last summer were attributed to shifts in ocean currents.'
To make more noticeable or prominent. Example: 'The report accentuates the need for renewable energy sources in developing nations.'
To provide what is needed or to adjust to something. Example: 'Universities must accommodate the diverse learning needs of an increasingly international student body.'
To gather or build up over time. Example: 'Researchers have accumulated substantial evidence linking air pollution to respiratory diseases.'
To stick firmly to a surface, or to follow rules or beliefs closely. Example: 'All participants in the study were required to adhere strictly to the prescribed dietary guidelines.'
The arrival or emergence of something notable. Example: 'The advent of artificial intelligence has transformed the landscape of modern healthcare.'
Harmful or unfavourable. Example: 'Prolonged exposure to noise pollution can have adverse effects on both mental and physical health.'
Concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty. Example: 'The aesthetic value of urban green spaces contributes significantly to residents' well-being.'
To make suffering or a problem less severe. Example: 'Government subsidies can alleviate the financial burden on low-income families seeking higher education.'
To combine or unite to form one structure or organisation. Example: 'The two research departments amalgamated to form a single interdisciplinary centre.'
Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something. Example: 'Many citizens remain ambivalent about the proposed changes to the national curriculum.'

Comparable in certain respects, typically in a way that makes clearer the nature of the things compared. Example: 'The relationship between a teacher and student is analogous to that of a mentor and apprentice.'
Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected. Example: 'The sudden drop in unemployment figures was regarded as a statistical anomaly rather than a lasting trend.'
The direct opposite of something. Example: 'The candidate's policies were the antithesis of what environmental groups had been advocating.'
To understand or perceive something, or to arrest someone. Example: 'Students often struggle to apprehend the complexities of quantum mechanics without practical demonstrations.'
Involving or requiring strenuous effort; difficult and tiring. Example: 'The arduous process of obtaining ethics approval delayed the research project by several months.'
To express an idea or feeling fluently and coherently. Example: 'The professor was able to articulate complex theories in a way that was accessible to all students.'
To find out for certain; to make sure of. Example: 'Further investigation is needed to ascertain whether the new drug has any long-term side effects.'
To absorb and integrate information, people, or ideas. Example: 'Immigrants who assimilate into a new culture often retain key elements of their original heritage.'
To make something greater by adding to it; to increase. Example: 'The university plans to augment its scholarship programme to attract more international students.'
Conducive to success; favourable. Example: 'The strong initial results provided an auspicious start to the five-year research initiative.'
Having the freedom to act independently or self-governing. Example: 'Autonomous learning is increasingly emphasised in higher education as a key skill for lifelong development.'
To prevent or turn away from something undesirable. Example: 'Swift policy intervention helped avert a full-scale economic recession in the region.'

A standard or point of reference against which things may be compared or assessed. Example: 'The country's literacy rate serves as a benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of its education system.'
To support, strengthen, or reinforce. Example: 'Recent findings bolster the argument that early childhood education has lasting cognitive benefits.'
Concise and exact use of words in writing or speech; shortness of time. Example: 'Academic writing values brevity, so candidates should avoid unnecessary repetition in their essays.'
A system of government or management marked by excessive rules and procedures. Example: 'Excessive bureaucracy in the healthcare system often delays patients' access to essential treatments.'
To adjust precisely for a particular function or to mark with a standard scale. Example: 'Researchers must calibrate their instruments carefully to ensure the accuracy of experimental data.'
A person or thing that precipitates an event or change. Example: 'The introduction of free public transport acted as a catalyst for reducing urban air pollution.'
To find a way around an obstacle or to overcome a problem cleverly. Example: 'Some corporations attempt to circumvent environmental regulations by relocating their factories overseas.'
To come together to form one mass or whole. Example: 'Several smaller advocacy groups coalesced into a single movement demanding climate action.'
To persuade someone to do something by using force or threats. Example: 'Ethical research guidelines prohibit investigators from coercing participants into joining a study.'
Clear, logical, and convincing. Example: 'The barrister presented a cogent argument that persuaded the jury to reconsider the evidence.'
Logical and consistent; forming a unified whole. Example: 'A coherent thesis statement is essential for achieving a high score in the IELTS writing task.'
To work jointly with others on an activity or project. Example: 'Scientists from multiple countries collaborated on the study to ensure a diverse data set.'
Used in ordinary or informal conversation; not formal. Example: 'While colloquial language is acceptable in the speaking test, academic writing demands a more formal register.'
Showing smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements. Example: 'Nations that become complacent about their economic success risk falling behind in global innovation.'
To add to something in a way that enhances or improves it. Example: 'Practical laboratory sessions complement theoretical lectures by providing hands-on experience.'
Making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible. Example: 'A quiet environment is conducive to focused study and improved academic performance.'
An opinion or conclusion formed on the basis of incomplete information. Example: 'Without sufficient data, any explanation for the decline in bee populations remains mere conjecture.'
Wishing to do one's work or duty well and thoroughly. Example: 'Conscientious students tend to perform better because they review material consistently rather than cramming.'
To make something stronger or more solid; to combine several things into one. Example: 'The government sought to consolidate its various welfare programmes into a single, more efficient system.'
Standing out so as to be clearly visible; attracting notice. Example: 'The conspicuous absence of women in senior management roles has prompted calls for policy reform.'
Dependent on certain conditions being met; occurring by chance. Example: 'Funding for the project is contingent upon the researchers meeting their first-year milestones.'
To come together from different directions to meet at a point. Example: 'Multiple lines of evidence converge to support the theory that exercise improves cognitive function.'
Extremely complex and difficult to follow. Example: 'The convoluted tax code makes it challenging for small business owners to file their returns accurately.'
To confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding. Example: 'Subsequent experiments corroborated the initial findings, lending greater credibility to the hypothesis.'
To reach a climax or point of highest development. Example: 'Years of diplomatic negotiations culminated in the signing of a historic peace agreement.'
To reduce in extent or quantity; to cut short. Example: 'Budget cuts forced the university to curtail its funding for postgraduate research.'
A scarcity or lack of something. Example: 'There is a dearth of qualified teachers in rural areas, which negatively affects educational outcomes.'
To make someone or something very weak. Example: 'Chronic stress can debilitate the immune system, leaving individuals more susceptible to illness.'
To arrive at a conclusion by reasoning from evidence. Example: 'From the survey results, researchers were able to deduce that income level correlates with access to healthcare.'
Not having enough of a specified quality or ingredient; lacking. Example: 'Diets deficient in essential vitamins can lead to serious health problems over time.'
To describe or portray something precisely. Example: 'The report delineates the key factors contributing to urban sprawl in rapidly developing countries.'
To publicly declare to be wrong or evil; to condemn. Example: 'Several human rights organisations denounced the new legislation as a violation of civil liberties.'
To represent or show something in a picture, story, or description. Example: 'The documentary depicts the harsh realities of life in communities affected by industrial pollution.'
To use up the supply or resources of something. Example: 'Overfishing has severely depleted marine stocks in several of the world's most productive oceans.'
To diminish in value over time. Example: 'Assets such as vehicles and machinery depreciate significantly within the first few years of purchase.'
To become progressively worse. Example: 'Air quality in the capital has continued to deteriorate despite the introduction of emission controls.'
Tending to cause harm. Example: 'Excessive screen time has been shown to have detrimental effects on children's attention spans.'
To depart from an established course or norm. Example: 'Researchers who deviate from the approved methodology risk compromising the validity of their study.'

A division or contrast between two things that are represented as being opposed or entirely different. Example: 'The dichotomy between economic growth and environmental sustainability remains a central challenge for policymakers.'
To perceive or recognise something, often with difficulty. Example: 'It can be difficult to discern reliable information from misinformation in the digital age.'
A lack of compatibility or similarity between two or more facts. Example: 'The discrepancy between the two data sets raised questions about the reliability of the original study.'
Essentially different in kind; not able to be compared. Example: 'The study examined disparate communities across three continents to identify common health challenges.'
To spread information, knowledge, or ideas widely. Example: 'Academic journals serve as a primary means to disseminate research findings to the scholarly community.'
To separate from another route or to differ in opinion or approach. Example: 'Expert opinions diverge on whether standardised testing accurately measures student ability.'
Temporarily inactive or not in use. Example: 'The volcano had been dormant for over a century before showing renewed signs of seismic activity.'
Hesitating or doubting; not to be relied upon. Example: 'The claims made in the advertisement are dubious and lack any supporting scientific evidence.'
The ability to produce a desired or intended result. Example: 'Clinical trials are essential for establishing the efficacy of a new vaccine before public distribution.'
To draw out a response or reaction from someone. Example: 'The interviewer's open-ended questions were designed to elicit detailed responses from the participants.'
To make something clear; to explain. Example: 'The professor used several case studies to elucidate the principles of behavioural economics.'
Difficult to find, catch, or achieve. Example: 'A lasting solution to urban homelessness has proven elusive despite decades of policy interventions.'
Based on observation or experience rather than theory or pure logic. Example: 'The study provides empirical evidence that bilingual education enhances cognitive flexibility in children.'
To surround or include comprehensively. Example: 'The new curriculum encompasses a wide range of subjects, from the sciences to the performing arts.'
